title: Intro to Numerical Analysis
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 200L Introduction to Numerical Analysis curriculum: sources of numerical error, root-finding methods (bisection, Newton-Raphson, secant), polynomial interpolation, numerical differentiation and integration, and numerical solution of linear systems.

questions.question: Round-off error in numerical computation arises primarily because:
options: Computers represent real numbers with a finite number of digits
The chosen numerical method is always incorrect
Only integers can be stored in memory
The algorithm never converges
questions.correct_answer: Computers represent real numbers with a finite number of digits
questions.explanation: Finite-precision (floating-point) representation cannot exactly store most real numbers, causing small representation errors that accumulate.

questions.question: Truncation error in numerical methods results from:
options: Approximating an infinite or exact mathematical process by a finite procedure
Rounding numbers to fewer decimal digits
Hardware malfunction
Using too many iterations
questions.correct_answer: Approximating an infinite or exact mathematical process by a finite procedure
questions.explanation: Truncation error comes from replacing an exact process, such as an infinite Taylor series, with a finite approximation, e.g. stopping a series after a few terms.

questions.question: The absolute error in an approximation is defined as:
options: |true value − approximate value|
true value / approximate value
true value × approximate value
approximate value − true value only when positive
questions.correct_answer: |true value − approximate value|
questions.explanation: Absolute error is the magnitude of the difference between the exact and approximate values.

questions.question: The Bisection Method for finding roots of f(x) = 0 requires that:
options: f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs on the interval [a, b], with f continuous
f must be differentiable everywhere
f(a) = f(b)
The interval [a, b] must contain no roots
questions.correct_answer: f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs on the interval [a, b], with f continuous
questions.explanation: The method relies on the Intermediate Value Theorem, which requires continuity and a sign change to guarantee a root exists within [a, b].

questions.question: In the Bisection Method, each iteration narrows the interval containing the root by a factor of:
questions.explanation: Bisection always splits the current interval in half, choosing the sub-interval where the sign change still occurs.

questions.question: The Newton-Raphson iteration formula for finding a root of f(x) = 0 is:
options: x(n+1) = xn − f(xn)/f'(xn)
x(n+1) = xn + f(xn)/f'(xn)
x(n+1) = xn − f'(xn)/f(xn)
x(n+1) = f(xn) − xn
questions.correct_answer: x(n+1) = xn − f(xn)/f'(xn)
questions.explanation: Newton-Raphson uses the tangent line at xn to produce the next approximation, subtracting f(xn) divided by the derivative f'(xn).

questions.question: A key drawback of the Newton-Raphson method compared to bisection is that:
options: It may fail to converge if the initial guess is poor or f'(x) is near zero
It always converges more slowly than bisection
It cannot be used on polynomial functions
It requires the interval to bracket the root
questions.correct_answer: It may fail to converge if the initial guess is poor or f'(x) is near zero
questions.explanation: Unlike bisection's guaranteed (though slow) convergence, Newton-Raphson can diverge or oscillate if the initial guess is far from the root or the derivative is very small.

questions.question: The Secant Method approximates the derivative in Newton's method using:
options: A finite difference between two previous iterates
The exact analytical derivative
The second derivative of f
A constant value of 1
questions.correct_answer: A finite difference between two previous iterates
questions.explanation: The secant method replaces f'(xn) with the slope of the secant line through the last two approximations, avoiding the need for an explicit derivative.

questions.question: Compared to the Bisection Method, the Newton-Raphson method (when it converges) typically converges:
options: Faster, since it has quadratic convergence versus bisection's linear convergence
Slower, since it needs more function evaluations
At the same rate as bisection
Only for linear functions
questions.correct_answer: Faster, since it has quadratic convergence versus bisection's linear convergence
questions.explanation: Newton-Raphson exhibits quadratic convergence near a simple root, roughly doubling the number of correct digits each iteration, much faster than bisection's linear rate.

questions.question: Polynomial interpolation seeks to:
options: Find a polynomial that passes exactly through a given set of data points
Compute the derivative of a function at a point
Solve a system of linear equations
Find the roots of an equation
questions.correct_answer: Find a polynomial that passes exactly through a given set of data points
questions.explanation: Interpolation constructs a function (typically polynomial) that exactly matches known data values, useful for estimating values between them.

questions.question: For n+1 distinct data points, the Lagrange interpolating polynomial has degree at most:
options: n
2n
questions.correct_answer: n
questions.explanation: Given n+1 distinct points, there is a unique interpolating polynomial of degree at most n passing through them.

questions.question: The Lagrange interpolating polynomial through points (x0, y0) and (x1, y1) is a straight line given by:
options: y0 + y1
y0x + y1
questions.explanation: This is the two-point Lagrange form, which is equivalent to the usual linear interpolation formula and passes through both given points.

questions.question: Newton's divided-difference interpolation formula is preferred over Lagrange's in some applications because:
options: New data points can be added without recomputing the entire polynomial from scratch
It always gives a lower-degree polynomial
It does not require distinct x-values
It avoids the use of any function values
questions.correct_answer: New data points can be added without recomputing the entire polynomial from scratch
questions.explanation: Newton's divided-difference form builds the polynomial incrementally, so adding an extra point just appends another term rather than restarting the calculation.

questions.question: The forward difference approximation for the first derivative of f at x0 with step size h is:
questions.explanation: The forward difference formula uses the function value at x0 and one step ahead, x0 + h, divided by the step size.

questions.question: The central difference approximation for f'(x0) is generally more accurate than the forward difference because:
options: Its truncation error is O(h²) rather than O(h)
It requires fewer function evaluations
It does not depend on the step size h
It is only usable for polynomials
questions.correct_answer: Its truncation error is O(h²) rather than O(h)
questions.explanation: The central difference formula [f(x0+h) − f(x0−h)]/(2h) has a smaller order of truncation error compared to the one-sided forward or backward differences.

questions.question: The Trapezoidal Rule approximates a definite integral by:
options: Approximating the area under the curve using trapezoids between sample points
Using rectangles of equal height
Fitting a cubic polynomial to every three points
Ignoring the function values at the endpoints
questions.correct_answer: Approximating the area under the curve using trapezoids between sample points
questions.explanation: The trapezoidal rule connects consecutive data points with straight lines, forming trapezoids whose areas approximate the integral.

questions.question: Using the Trapezoidal Rule with a single interval [a, b], the approximate integral of f is:
options: (b−a) × f(a)
questions.explanation: The single-interval trapezoidal rule averages the endpoint function values and multiplies by the interval width.

questions.question: Simpson's 1/3 Rule for numerical integration requires that the interval be divided into:
options: An even number of equal subintervals
An odd number of equal subintervals
Exactly three subintervals only
Unequal subintervals
questions.correct_answer: An even number of equal subintervals
questions.explanation: Simpson's 1/3 rule fits parabolas over pairs of subintervals, so it requires an even total number of equal-width subintervals.

questions.question: Compared to the Trapezoidal Rule, Simpson's Rule is generally more accurate because it:
options: Approximates the integrand with parabolic (quadratic) segments instead of straight lines
Uses fewer function evaluations
Ignores the endpoints of the interval
Only works for linear functions
questions.correct_answer: Approximates the integrand with parabolic (quadratic) segments instead of straight lines
questions.explanation: By fitting quadratics rather than linear segments, Simpson's Rule captures curvature better and has a smaller truncation error, O(h⁴) versus O(h²).

questions.question: In Gaussian elimination applied numerically, partial pivoting is used to:
options: Reduce round-off error by avoiding division by very small pivot elements
Increase the size of the matrix
Guarantee the system has no solution
Convert the system into a nonlinear one
questions.correct_answer: Reduce round-off error by avoiding division by very small pivot elements
questions.explanation: Partial pivoting swaps rows to place the largest available element in the pivot position, improving numerical stability.

questions.question: The Jacobi iterative method for solving Ax = b updates each variable using:
options: Only the values from the previous iteration for all other variables
The most recently updated values within the same iteration
A random initial guess with no formula
Only the diagonal entries of A, ignoring b
questions.correct_answer: Only the values from the previous iteration for all other variables
questions.explanation: In the Jacobi method, all components are updated simultaneously using values from the prior iteration, unlike Gauss-Seidel which uses updated values immediately.

questions.question: The Gauss-Seidel method differs from the Jacobi method in that it:
options: Uses the most recently computed values of variables immediately within the same iteration
Never converges for diagonally dominant matrices
Requires no initial guess
Cannot be applied to linear systems
questions.correct_answer: Uses the most recently computed values of variables immediately within the same iteration
questions.explanation: Gauss-Seidel updates each variable in place and uses the newest available values right away, typically making it converge faster than Jacobi.

questions.question: A sufficient condition for both Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel iterations to converge is that the coefficient matrix A is:
options: Strictly diagonally dominant
The zero matrix
Singular
Symmetric only, with no other conditions
questions.correct_answer: Strictly diagonally dominant
questions.explanation: If in each row the magnitude of the diagonal entry exceeds the sum of the magnitudes of the other entries, both iterative methods are guaranteed to converge.

questions.question: Using the Bisection Method on f(x) = x² − 4 with initial interval [0, 3], the first midpoint tested is:
questions.explanation: The midpoint of [0, 3] is (0+3)/2 = 1.5, which is the first approximation tested in bisection.

questions.question: In fixed-point iteration for solving x = g(x), convergence to the fixed point is guaranteed near x0 if:
options: |g'(x)| < 1 in a neighborhood of the fixed point
g(x) is any continuous function
g'(x) > 1 near the fixed point
questions.correct_answer: |g'(x)| < 1 in a neighborhood of the fixed point
questions.explanation: The fixed-point iteration xn+1 = g(xn) converges locally when the derivative of g has magnitude less than 1 near the fixed point.

questions.question: What order of convergence does the Secant Method have, compared to Newton's method's quadratic (order 2) convergence?
options: Approximately 1.618 (the golden ratio), superlinear but sub-quadratic
Exactly order 3 (cubic)
Exactly order 1 (linear), same as bisection
It does not converge at all
questions.correct_answer: Approximately 1.618 (the golden ratio), superlinear but sub-quadratic
questions.explanation: The secant method has an order of convergence equal to the golden ratio φ ≈ 1.618, faster than linear methods but slightly slower than Newton's quadratic convergence.

questions.question: Relative error is generally preferred over absolute error when comparing approximations because:
options: It accounts for the scale/magnitude of the quantity being measured
It is always smaller than absolute error
It ignores the true value entirely
It cannot be negative
questions.correct_answer: It accounts for the scale/magnitude of the quantity being measured
questions.explanation: Relative error (|true − approx| / |true|) gives a scale-independent measure, so errors on very large or very small quantities can be meaningfully compared.

questions.question: For the function f(x) = x³ − x − 2, evaluate f(1) and f(2) to determine if a root lies in [1, 2].
options: f(1) = −2, f(2) = 4, so a root lies in [1, 2] by the sign change
f(1) = 0, f(2) = 0, so there is no root
f(1) and f(2) are both positive, so no root exists in [1,2]
f(1) and f(2) are both negative
questions.correct_answer: f(1) = −2, f(2) = 4, so a root lies in [1, 2] by the sign change
questions.explanation: f(1) = 1 − 1 − 2 = −2 and f(2) = 8 − 2 − 2 = 4; since the signs differ, the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees a root in (1, 2).

questions.question: Increasing the number of subintervals in the Trapezoidal or Simpson's Rule generally:
options: Reduces truncation error but may increase accumulated round-off error
Has no effect on accuracy
Always reduces total error without limit
Eliminates all numerical error entirely
questions.correct_answer: Reduces truncation error but may increase accumulated round-off error
questions.explanation: Finer subdivision improves the approximation to the true integral (lower truncation error) but requires more arithmetic operations, which can accumulate round-off error.

questions.question: Using Simpson's 1/3 Rule with two subintervals [x0, x1, x2] of equal width h, the approximate integral is:
questions.explanation: Simpson's 1/3 rule on a single pair of subintervals weights the middle ordinate by 4 and the endpoints by 1, all scaled by h/3.
